citations.quote: This paper presents the development of a general automated process using multibody dynamics software (RecurDyn), to efficiently take a detailed hinge assembly model and simulate its range of motion while retrieving stiffness information for all degrees of freedom and use that data to define a simple but accurate, nonlinear point-to-point force for use in a solar array assembly model.
The second objective is the development and simulation of a high-

fidelity system-level model of the deployment dynamics of a commercial deployable solar array that was designed for use with a 6U cubesat. First a detailed model of the hinge assembly will be constructed, using finite element meshes to define portions of the hinge components as flexible, and including any necessary contacts between those components. The vertical application then presents a dialog to the user to enable him or her to set-up the model quickly for stiffness testing. The application then carries out a series of automated simulations to test the stiffness of the hinge and also rotates the hinge 90 degrees to capture the same information with the hinge in the vertical orientation. Once the simulations are done the vertical application will sort through the output data to calculate the hinge's stiffness for each DOF, and that information will be used to define a RecurDyn userfunction Screw force entity that is an efficient point-to-point force.
The vertical application is executed through three tasks. These are 1) the Run Hinge Simulation task, 2) the Review Hinge Simulation Results task, and 3) the Create Simplified Hinge Force task.

The dialog allows the user to define the base and action bodies as well as specify which simulations, to run. The user can also specify the peak force or torque applied for each simulation. The Set Up and Run button commands the vertical application to run the simulations specified by the user. For each simulation, the force(s) or torque(s) will be applied with magnitudes that vary between the positive and negative values of the max force or torque specified in the dialog box. The general pattern of an applied force is shown in fig. 6. For each direction that a force or torque is applied the simulation is run with the hinge in both the horizontal and vertical position, as shown in fig. 7. During the simulation the displacement of the action side of the hinge is predicted and force vs. displacement or torque vs. rotation information is stored as a spline in the hinge model database.

The final task is the Create Simplified Hinge force in System Model task. This task allows the user to command the vertical development application to integrate the hinge characterization simulation data into a system level model. To execute the task, the Create Simplified Hinge Force icon is chosen from the ribbon menu in RecurDyn. When the user clicks on this icon, the dialog shown at right in Figure 9 is displayed. The dialog enables the user to easily select from the modeling window the bodies that will connect to the simplified hinge force, as well as the locations of those connections and intended orientations of the hinge halves. When the user clicks on the Apply button, the vertical application will create a new subsystem within the system level model that contains the simplified hinge force, as shown below in Figure 10. The subsystem, shown in Figure 11, will contain a base and action dummy body that are connected with a RecurDyn Screw Force, which can exert forces or torques from one body to another in all six degrees of freedom, with each force or torque being defined by an expression. The vertical application will align the subsystem with the base marker selected by the user, and the action dummy body within the subsystem will be oriented to align with the action marker selected by the user. A fixed joint will be created between the base body in the system level model and the base dummy body within the subsystem, as well as between the action body in the system level model and the action dummy body within the subsystem.
The subsystem can be exported to a file which can be stored and imported into a different model. This capability allows the user to develop a library of hinges.

The expressions controlling the component forces and torques of the screw force were formulated to simulate the reaction force of the hinge, based on the hinge characterization simulations. The formulation enforces radial behavior so that both x- and y-axis translation are considered simultaneously and not independently when calculating the reaction forces. (The same consideration is made for x- and y-axis rotation.) This is needed because a gap typically exists between hinge components, allowing for free movement of the components before any deflection begins. To demonstrate this, in Figure 12 below, a translational force of constant magnitude but rotating direction is applied to the action body shown in red, in order to take the action body through its path of free motion. With a non-radial formulation, the path of motion is erroneously square and overestimates the amount of gap at the diagonal positions. But with the radial formulation, the path of motion is correctly circular in shape.

A system level model of the e-HaWK solar array was constructed in RecurDyn. This model was used to characterize the deployment process and evaluate the sensitivity of the design to various input parameters. This process was broken up into the following steps; 1) flexible body representation of the solar panels, 2) storage, 3) deployment characterization, and 4) simulation trials.

The panel mesh was fixed to the hinges using RecurDyn Force Distributing Rigid (FDR) elements (equivalent to Nastran RBE2 elements) using the nodes immediately surrounding the hinge. This was then tested using a 1g drop test to determine the viability of the mesh and the attachment to the hinge. The hinges were fixed to ground and the panel dropped 20 degrees before impacting the bump stops. The first impact with the bump stops is shown in Figure 14. In this image it can be seen that the majority of the stress is distributed through the frame as expected. Stress concentrations occur near the hinges where the load is being applied and in the middle where the frame narrows to a small cross section. This was determined to be an acceptable mesh for the system level model.
This was achieved in two steps. First, the system was folded with all contacts inactive. Second, the contacts were activated and the system was given time to settle.

After approximately 1 second the center panel has extended 90 degrees and the root hinges impact the bump stops. Very little vibration is seen as the panel-to-panel hinges impact the bump stops. The solar array is fully deployed in 1.9 seconds and after 2.6 seconds the residual motion in the material has dampened out. The amount of vibration at impact is highly dependent upon the damping parameter at the contact. If necessary, this parameter can be adjusted to match results in a validation study.

Figure 19 shows the force on the hinge during changes in angular acceleration. In fig. 19 the angular acceleration is ramped up quickly to keep the angular velocity negligible. The results from a ramped up angular velocity applied at the center of mass can be seen in fig. 22. The side panel decoupled from the hard stop at an angular acceleration of 11.8 rad/s^2.

In order to capture the effect of the hinges, this same test was applied with hinges that were free to rotate. This necessitated using a smaller force to avoid complete decoupling of the hard stops. The results of this test are shown in fig. 22. This test resulted in a fundamental frequency of approximately 3 Hz. However, this motion dampened fast enough that only one period could be evaluated.

A set of 11 trials was run to evaluate the sensitivity of the model to various input factors. The five input factors that were evaluated are root spring stiffness, panel-panel spring stiffness, side panel substrate modulus, center panel substrate modulus, and solar array add-on mass. Parameters were adjusted by 20% from the nominal value. The study was conducted with the intention of being used to develop physical test to validate the performance of the simulations.

Increasing the spring stiffness tends to decrease time to deploy and increases stability while deployed while increasing the solar array add-on mass increased the time to deploy and decreased stability while deployed. However, trial 1 seems to be an outlier to these trends. Examining the simulation results for this case reveals an oscillation in the residual stresses of the left panel that is timed in such a way that the deployment of the left panel is delayed.
